---
title: "Developing and testing a theory"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = FALSE, comment = "")
# Console colour carries no meaning on a rendered page. pkgdown turns it on for
# its own build, and the escape sequences then reach the reader as literal text,
# so colour is switched off here for a plain vignette render and a site build
# alike. The fixed width keeps printed output inside the documentation column.
options(cli.num_colors = 1, cli.hyperlink = FALSE, crayon.enabled = FALSE,
        width = 80)
# Both optional packages are needed to turn the DOT source into an inline
# SVG, so the rendering chunks below are skipped when either is absent.
has_diagram <- requireNamespace("DiagrammeR", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("DiagrammeRsvg", quietly = TRUE)
library(theoryforge)
```

The Get started vignette reads, validates, scores and builds a theory. This
article continues with the stages of developing and testing it. It appraises an
amendment, derives what the theory's causal graph commits it to, compares the
theory with a rival, writes the theory and hypotheses sections of a
preregistration, grades a test after the data and assembles the dossier.
The examples read the theories that ship with the package through
`tf_example_path()`, so every chunk needs only `theoryforge`, apart from those
that draw a diagram with `tf_render_diagram()`, which also need the optional
DiagrammeR and DiagrammeRsvg packages and are skipped without them.

## Developing: appraising an amendment

A theory changes as it meets data, and the question is whether a change
strengthens it. `tf_appraise_amendment()` compares an amended version with its
prior version, the version before the new predictions were stated, and
classifies the change as progressive, degenerating or neutral, by fixed rules
that borrow the terms of Lakatos's methodology of research programmes.

```{r appraise}
v1 <- tf_read(tf_example_path("panic-network.theory.yaml"))
v2 <- tf_read(tf_example_path("panic-network-2026-v2.theory.yaml"))

appraisal <- tf_appraise_amendment(v2, v1)
str(appraisal[c("verdict", "new_predictions", "corroborated_new", "dropped",
                "ad_hoc_assumptions", "content_lost", "implications_lost",
                "implications_lost_unrefuted", "signs_lost")])
```

The first version implies that arousal and avoidance are independent given
perceived threat and states that independence as `pred_indep`, which a test
refuted. The second drops `pred_indep`, adds a direct path from arousal to
avoidance and derives from it a new prediction that a registered test
corroborates. It gives up one implied independence, the refuted one. It also
gives up a sign. Both versions say that perceived threat causes arousal without
saying in which direction, so in the second version the new path opens a route
from threat to avoidance through arousal whose sign is not stated. The first
version entails that raising perceived threat raises avoidance, and the second
does not, so the amendment loses unrefuted content and is `neutral`. Stating
that threat increases arousal in both versions would make it `progressive`.

The verdict is `progressive` when a corroborated new prediction adds content, no
content is lost, no ad hoc assumption is added, no corroborated prediction is
dropped and no failed prediction is weakened. It is never `progressive` when the
causal graph of either version cannot be read, since the content of the two
cannot then be compared. It is `degenerating` when an ad hoc assumption is added
or a failed prediction is weakened and no corroborated new prediction adds
content. Any other combination is `neutral`, theoryforge's label for an
amendment that meets neither rule. A new prediction adds no content when it
derives from no proposition or only articulates what the prior version already
held, and a prediction under a new id with the same statement and type is
reported as `renamed`. An assumption added for an anomaly is ad hoc when it
protects no new prediction other than that anomaly, or when some of those
predictions have been tested and none is corroborated. While all of them are
untested, it is `pending`. An assumption rewritten under its id is appraised as
a new one is, and one moved unchanged to another id is not appraised. Any change
of wording counts, even one that keeps the meaning, so a core assumption
reworded under its id is appraised and, when it protects a prediction that
failed in the prior, is read as answering it. Each appraised assumption that
answers an anomaly is listed in `assumptions` with its `change`, `new` or
`revised`.

The verdict holds only if what the two files declare is true, the test outcomes
and the `added_for` and `protects` of each assumption above all. The appraisal
reads no dates and nothing about where the data came from, so it cannot tell a
prediction from an accommodation of data already seen, and deciding which
version is the prior is the caller's responsibility. Read `refuted_new` and
`corroborated_new_severity` with the verdict: one corroborated new prediction
among many that failed, or a pass whose own estimate lies outside the claimed
region, is enough for `progressive`. `?tf_appraise_amendment` lists the other
fields of the result, and the article 'Methodological foundations' gives the
full rule.

## Testing

Testing starts from what the theory commits itself to. The testing sections
read the modality-switching theory, whose causal graph is acyclic. Three of its
four predictions and its one phenomenon state machine-readable claims, and its
two rivals state propositions of their own. Where a feedback loop matters, the
sections read the panic-network theory instead.

```{r switching}
switching <- tf_read(tf_example_path("modality-switching.theory.yaml"))
```

### The claim-form rubric

`tf_severity()` grades each prediction before any data, by the form of its
claim. The base risk rises with the strength of the claim, from `existence` to
`point`. A directional prediction is discounted for the correlations a field
shows anyway, and a prediction that names a registered rival in `diagnostic_vs`
gains a small bonus.

```{r severity}
tf_severity(switching)
```

The values, the discount and the bonus are the package's conventions. The
rubric reads only the declared type and the named rivals, so it ranks claims by
their form and says nothing about how severely a claim has been tested, which
depends on the design and the data. Post-data severity, further below, reads
the data.

### What the causal graph implies

A theory's propositions together form a graph, and the graph implies
conditional independencies that the theory does not state. `tf_implications()`
derives them. Each directed relation is an arrow, and an association is a
bidirected edge, covariance the theory leaves unexplained. The graph is read as
complete: every pair of constructs in it that no proposition joins is read as
having no direct effect on each other and no unexplained association. Every
such pair yields one statement when some set of other constructs separates it,
usually the parents of both. The statements are consequences of the graph as
encoded, so they are the theory's commitments only if its authors meant those
omissions. When every relation is directed, these statements are the basis set,
from which every other independence the graph implies follows when the
distribution has the composition property, as a multivariate normal one does.

```{r implications}
statements <- function(implied) {
  writeLines(vapply(implied$implications, function(i) i$statement, character(1)))
}
statements(tf_implications(switching))
```

Switch cost and conceptual access are the two children of a fork at modality
activation, so the theory says that their correlation is due to that shared
cause and vanishes once it is held fixed. Sensorimotor experience and lexical
familiarity meet only at the collider at conceptual access, so the theory says
they are unrelated with nothing held fixed. The first statement is not among
the theory's predictions, whereas the second is stated as `pred4`. Evidence
against either would count against the theory as encoded, including the
omissions the statement rests on.

The basis set conditions on the parents of both constructs, which can be more
than a single test needs. `given = "minimal"` prunes each conditioning set until
none of its members can be dropped.

```{r implications-minimal}
statements(tf_implications(switching, given = "minimal"))
```

A minimal set holds fewer constructs, and that matters because the constructs
are measured with error. Error in a conditioning construct leaves part of the
dependence that holding it fixed should remove, so a conditional statement
tested on observed scores is rejected too often, and more often the larger the
sample ([Westfall & Yarkoni, 2016](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0152719)).
Take a chain whose two paths have standardised coefficients of .5, with the
middle construct measured at a reliability of .8. The chunk below computes the
partial correlation of the two ends given the observed middle and the rate at
which a test at the 5 per cent level rejects the true statement.

```{r measurement-error}
r_observed <- 0.5 * sqrt(0.8)            # each end with the observed middle
partial <- (0.5 * 0.5 - r_observed^2) / (1 - r_observed^2)
n <- c(200, 500, 1000)
z <- atanh(partial) * sqrt(n - 4)
data.frame(n = n, partial = round(partial, 4),
           rejected = round(pnorm(z - 1.96) + pnorm(-z - 1.96), 2))
```

The minimal statements suit tests of single pairs. They are no longer a basis
set, so their tests are not to be combined into one test of the model, as the
tests of a basis set can be. A conditional statement is better tested in a
latent-variable model, which takes the measurement error into account, and each
statement can be tested in such a model separately
([Thoemmes et al., 2018](https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000147)).

A graph with a feedback loop is refused by default. The panic-network theory has
a loop between arousal and perceived threat.

```{r implications-cycle, error = TRUE}
tf_implications(v1)
```

```{r implications-sigma}
looped <- tf_implications(v1, cycles = "sigma")
lapply(looped$feedback, unlist)
statements(looped)
```

The d-separation criterion, which dagitty applies to any graph, is guaranteed to
hold in a model with feedback only in special cases, a linear model among them.
Sigma-separation holds whenever each feedback loop settles into a unique
equilibrium ([Bongers et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.1214/21-AOS2064)), and
`cycles = "sigma"` applies it. A theory that posits alternative stable states,
such as a calm state and a panic state that each sustain themselves, violates
that assumption, and its statements are then not guaranteed.

### What the causal graph entails

A prediction or a phenomenon can state its claim in machine-readable form, as
the effect of one construct on another or the association between two, with a
sign.

```{r claim}
str(switching$predictions[[1]]$claim)
```

`tf_entailments()` reads each claim against the graph. The signs of the routes
between the two constructs decide whether the graph entails the claim,
contradicts it or leaves it undetermined, and `via` names the propositions the
verdict rests on. For an effect claim on an acyclic graph, `adjustment` gives a
smallest set of constructs whose adjustment would identify the effect in
observational data, or a minimal set when more than 12 constructs are
candidates. Here it is the empty set. For other claims, it is `NA`.
`identified` reports identification by adjustment alone, so an effect without
such a set may still be identified by other means, such as the front-door
criterion, and a set for a cause or an outcome marked latent assumes a measure
of it.

```{r entailments}
entailed <- tf_entailments(switching)
listed <- function(x) if (identical(x, NA)) NA_character_ else paste(unlist(x), collapse = ", ")
data.frame(
  id = vapply(entailed$claims, function(c) c$id, character(1)),
  kind = vapply(entailed$claims, function(c) c$kind, character(1)),
  sign = vapply(entailed$claims, function(c) c$sign, character(1)),
  verdict = vapply(entailed$claims, function(c) c$verdict, character(1)),
  via = vapply(entailed$claims, function(c) listed(c$via), character(1)),
  adjustment = vapply(entailed$claims, function(c) listed(c$adjustment), character(1))
)
```

The derived signs hold when the graph is the causal structure, with no common
cause of two constructs left out unless an association stands for it, and when
each directed relation acts in its stated direction whatever the other inputs,
as in a linear model or a uniformly monotone one. A verdict whose `faithfulness`
is `TRUE` also assumes that effects do not cancel exactly, along a route of
unknown sign or between routes of opposite signs, and the preregistration and
the dossier end its line with `unless effects cancel exactly`. Under
`cycles = "sigma"`, the sign of an effect further assumes that the system with
the intervened construct held fixed settles, which the stability of the system
as observed does not ensure. The function shows what the propositions commit the
theory to and does not show whether a claim holds in data. The checklist's
derivation-chain item counts a prediction whose claim the graph contradicts or
leaves open as not derived from the propositions it cites.

### Equivalent models

Graphs that imply the same conditional independencies are Markov equivalent, and
no test of conditional independence can tell them apart
([Andersson et al., 1997](https://doi.org/10.1214/aos/1031833662)). In
structural equation modelling, this is the problem of equivalent models
([MacCallum et al., 1993](https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.114.1.185)).
`tf_equivalent_models()` marks each directed edge as compelled, pointing the same
way in every equivalent graph, or reversible.

```{r equivalent}
equivalent <- tf_equivalent_models(switching)
str(equivalent$v_structures)
data.frame(
  proposition = vapply(equivalent$edges, function(e) listed(e$propositions), character(1)),
  from = vapply(equivalent$edges, function(e) e$from, character(1)),
  to = vapply(equivalent$edges, function(e) e$to, character(1)),
  status = vapply(equivalent$edges, function(e) e$status, character(1))
)
```

The collider at conceptual access compels the two edges into it. The other two
edges are reversible, so no test of conditional independence can tell whether
sensorimotor experience drives modality activation or the reverse. Telling the
direction apart needs an intervention, a temporal order or distributional
assumptions such as non-Gaussian errors. The function does not know which
constructs a study manipulates, so an edge out of a construct that an
experiment sets is listed as reversible all the same. The rule covers acyclic
graphs of directed relations, so for a theory with a feedback loop or an
association the record says why it was not computed.

```{r equivalent-loop}
tf_equivalent_models(v1)$reason
```

### Comparing the theory with a rival

A registered alternative can state its own propositions over the theory's
constructs, under `alternatives[].propositions`. In grounding by interaction,
perceptual activation follows access to the concept instead of feeding it.

```{r rival}
rival <- switching$alternatives[[1]]
do.call(rbind, lapply(rival$propositions, as.data.frame))
```

`tf_discriminate()` sets the two graphs side by side. It lists the claims of the
theory on which the two graphs give opposite verdicts, the independencies one
graph implies and the other does not, and the effects and associations whose
sign differs between them. Each of these is a result that could tell the two
accounts apart.

```{r discriminate}
compared <- tf_discriminate(switching, "alt_grounding_by_interaction")
compared$markov_equivalent
unlist(compared$counts)
do.call(rbind, lapply(compared$claims, as.data.frame))
writeLines(vapply(compared$independencies,
                  function(i) paste(i$implied_by, i$statement), character(1)))
```

The rival can also be a theory of its own, whose constructs are matched to the
theory's by id. The comparison reads only the propositions each account states
and does not say which account the data favour. The checklist's diagnosticity
item reads the same verdicts: a prediction that names a rival in `diagnostic_vs`
counts only when the rival's own graph does not give its claim the same verdict.

### Preregistration

`tf_preregister()` writes the theory and hypotheses sections of a
preregistration as Markdown. Its header gives the theory's version and content
hash and the status of the checklist's derivation chain, read with the
document's `cycles`, and, when the causal graph has a feedback loop, a line that
says whether the document refuses the loop or reads it by sigma-separation. A
line in italics then says what the document holds and what must be added before
registration. The hypotheses section opens with the assumptions that the
verdicts on the claims rest on. Each hypothesis is listed with its type, its
derivation, its claim and what the graph says of it, the adjustment an
observational test would need, the auxiliary assumptions that protect it, the
rivals it is declared to discriminate and its test record. The hypotheses
section of the modality-switching theory reads as follows.

```{r prereg}
prereg <- tf_preregister(switching)
start <- regexpr("## Hypotheses", prereg, fixed = TRUE)
end <- regexpr("## Sampling plan", prereg, fixed = TRUE)
cat(substr(prereg, start, end - 1))
```

A sampling plan section, the implied conditional independencies, with a line
that says they rest on the omissions of the graph, and a severity line for each
prediction follow. A registry also needs the study design, the
analysis plan and the inference criteria, which a theory file does not hold, and
a template such as PRP-QUANT sets them out
([Bosnjak et al., 2022](https://doi.org/10.1037/amp0000879)). Passing a `path`
also writes the document to disk, with LF line endings.

### Post-data severity

A prediction with `bounds` states the region of a quantity its claim allows,
and a test outcome can record the estimate the test observed and its standard
error. `tf_post_data_severity()` computes, for each such outcome, how severely
the claim passed. For a claim with one bound, it is the post-data severity of
[Mayo and Spanos (2006)](https://doi.org/10.1093/bjps/axl003): the probability
that the test would have given a result less in accord with the claim, had the
quantity been at the bound. For a claim with two bounds, it takes the smaller of
the two one-sided values, the package's own extension, which equals 1 minus the
p value of the z-based two one-sided tests of equivalence
([Lakens, 2017](https://doi.org/10.1177/1948550617697177)).

The theory's interval prediction for the switch cost records one outcome, with
illustrative values. A second outcome is added below, as a replication whose
estimate falls above the region.

```{r post-data-severity}
replicated <- tf_add_test_outcome(
  switching, "pred2", TRUE, estimate = 63, se = 6,
  observed = "Illustrative values: switch cost 63 ms (SE 6 ms)."
)
tf_post_data_severity(replicated)
```

The dossier writes each value beside its outcome in its test record. It writes
a value that rounds to 1 as `> 0.999` and one that rounds to 0 as `< 0.001`,
since a test cannot give certainty, and it marks an outcome recorded as passed
whose estimate lies outside the region and one recorded as failed whose
estimate lies inside it.

```{r dossier-test-record}
dossier <- tf_dossier(replicated)
start <- regexpr("## Test record", dossier, fixed = TRUE)
end <- regexpr("## Evidence", dossier, fixed = TRUE)
cat(substr(dossier, start, end - 1))
```

The computation uses a normal approximation and treats the standard error as
known, so it overstates the severity of an estimate inside the region when the
standard error comes from a small sample. The standard error must describe the
sampling distribution of the estimate at the bound. The value is nominal, so it
does not account for selection, such as a subgroup chosen after seeing the data,
and it does not check the statistical adequacy of the model behind the
estimate. A high value does not show that the claim is true, and the checklist
does not read it.

### The dossier

`tf_dossier()` assembles one Markdown document for a reviewer or an editor. Its
header gives the content hash, the checklist version, the checklist score with
its range and the gate, and, when the causal graph has a feedback loop, how the
dossier reads it. A paragraph in italics then says what the score describes,
what the gate checks and what the dossier is: the test outcomes, evidence,
registrations and declared severities are as the author recorded them, and the
dossier checks none of them beyond the inconsistencies it flags, so it is not an
independent audit. Sections on the checklist, where the two items that decide
the gate are marked `(blocker)`, the severities, the test record, the evidence,
the claims and the causal graph, the equivalent models for observational data,
the rivals and the provenance follow, and the preregistration closes it. The
same theory file gives the same dossier for the same `cycles`, so it can be
committed or attached to a submission. Its header and sections read as follows.

```{r dossier}
dossier <- tf_dossier(switching)
lines <- strsplit(dossier, "\n", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
writeLines(lines[seq_len(grep("^## Checklist", lines) - 1)])
grep("^## ", lines, value = TRUE)
```

### Compiling a measurement model

`tf_compile_sem()` writes lavaan model syntax for `lavaan::sem()` and does not
need lavaan installed. Constructs with indicators become latent variables with
`=~`, directed propositions labelled paths with `~` and associations covariances
with `~~`. Comments say whether the paths are identified, or what identifying
them would need, and list the sign each `increases` or `decreases` proposition
states, and the effect each claim is about is defined with `:=`, so that lavaan
estimates the quantity the claim concerns.

```{r sem}
cat(tf_compile_sem(switching))
```

The comment after the structural model says that its paths form no loop and that
no pair of constructs is joined by both a path and a covariance, so the path
coefficients are generically identified if the measurement model identifies the
constructs ([Brito & Pearl, 2002](https://doi.org/10.1207/s15328007sem0904_1)).
The last block fixes at zero the covariance of the two exogenous constructs and
the residual covariance of the two terminal ones, which two of the implied
independencies require. `lavaan::sem()` frees them by default, so a fit with its
defaults could not refute either statement, and deleting the block restores the
defaults. The indicator names are the measurement entries made safe for lavaan
and must match columns of the data. A construct with a single indicator is
treated as measured without error. A feedback loop makes the model
non-recursive, and such a model may not be identified
([Bollen, 1989](https://doi.org/10.1002/9781118619179)), so the syntax flags
each loop in a comment and is a starting point for a fit.

## Rendering and depositing

`tf_render_report()` writes the dossier as a Quarto source document, ready to
render to HTML or PDF. A theory file may come from someone else, so the header
tells Quarto to run no code, compile no OJS and load no MathJax, the theory's
text is escaped so that Quarto reads it as text, and a theory whose text Quarto
would decode as a shortcode is refused. With Quarto 1.11, reports of hostile
theory files rendered this way to html, revealjs and dashboard, and opened in a
browser that loaded their scripts and clicked their links, ran none of the
code, shortcodes or scripts the files held. The escaping holds for Quarto and
Pandoc alone: writers of other markup languages, such as `hugo-md`,
`docusaurus-md`, `org` or `mediawiki`, write the text back for programs that
can run it, so render such a file to `html`, `revealjs`, `dashboard`, `pdf`,
`typst`, `docx`, `odt`, `pptx` or `epub`. Quarto also runs the scripts and
filters that `_quarto.yml`, `_metadata.yml`, `_brand.yml` and `_extensions`
name in the report's folder or any folder above it, so write the report into a
folder of your own. With `render = FALSE`, the default, it writes the `.qmd`
without calling Quarto, and it returns the path of the file it wrote.

```{r render-report}
report_path <- tf_render_report(switching, tempfile(fileext = ".qmd"))
file.exists(report_path)
```

`tf_osf_push()` deposits the dossier on an Open Science Framework node, as
`<id>.dossier.md`. It defaults to `dry_run = TRUE`, which assembles the request
and returns it without sending anything, so the planned deposit can be inspected
offline and without a token.

```{r osf}
str(tf_osf_push(switching, node = "ab12c"))
```

A live deposit needs `dry_run = FALSE`, a personal access token, the node id and
the curl package. OSF refuses a second file with the same name, which
`tf_osf_push()` reports as an error with HTTP 409. Pass a filename that names the
version, or `overwrite = TRUE` to send the dossier to the existing file as a new
OSF version.

```{r osf-live, eval = FALSE}
tf_osf_push(switching, node = "ab12c", token = Sys.getenv("OSF_PAT"),
            dry_run = FALSE)
```

## Visualising the theory

`tf_diagram()` returns ten views of a theory. Seven are graphs written in
Graphviz DOT, or for the `causal_dag` view in DAGitty's syntax, and three are SVG
images. The Get started vignette shows the nomological network and the causal
graph. The views below draw the panic-network theory, which records test
outcomes and scope conditions, and each is drawn with `tf_render_diagram()`. The
`workflow` view traces the theory from its constructs through its propositions
and predictions to the recorded test outcomes.

```{r workflow-render, results = "asis", eval = has_diagram}
cat('<div class="tf-figure tf-diagram">',
    tf_render_diagram(v1, "workflow", as = "svg"), '</div>', sep = "")
```

The `context` view places the theory among its scope conditions and the rivals
it is meant to outpredict.

```{r context-render, results = "asis", eval = has_diagram}
cat('<div class="tf-figure tf-diagram">',
    tf_render_diagram(v1, "context", as = "svg"), '</div>', sep = "")
```

The `pipeline` view links each prediction to its test outcomes, one node for
each, so a failed replication appears beside the pass it followed. The
`provenance` view draws the provenance log.

```{r pipeline-render, results = "asis", eval = has_diagram}
cat('<div class="tf-figure tf-diagram">',
    tf_render_diagram(v1, "pipeline", as = "svg"), '</div>', sep = "")
```

The `venn`, `rigour` and `severity` views are returned as SVG. The `venn` view
draws the boundary conditions of the first three constructs as overlapping sets,
the `rigour` view the checklist as a grid of statuses and the `severity` view
one bar per prediction.

```{r rigour-view, results = "asis"}
cat('<div class="tf-figure">', tf_diagram(v1, "rigour"), '</div>', sep = "")
```

The `development_roadmap` view turns the checklist into a worklist. It keeps the
items that fail or warn and orders them as the work should be done: the items
that block the gate first, heaviest first, then the advisory ones. The weak
theory of the Get started vignette gives the full list, one numbered node for
each item.

```{r roadmap}
weak <- tf_read(tf_example_path("weak-theory.theory.yaml"))
cat(tf_diagram(weak, "development_roadmap"))
```

`?tf_diagram` documents each view.

## Simulation

`tf_simulate()` treats each construct as a state variable and propagates the
signed network of propositions as a linear dynamical system. `increases` couples
positively and `decreases` negatively. `causes` and `mediates` state no sign, so
they are coupled positively by an assumption the record lists under
`assumed_positive`, and `moderates` and `associates` are not coupled. A theory
states no parameter values, so the trajectory is that of one linear model
consistent with the signs the propositions state, with one gain `k` for every
coupling and a decay at the rate `damping` for every state. Each row is the
solution of the system at its time, computed with the matrix exponential,
whatever the step size.

The example closes a loop in which avoidance lowers arousal. The run covers 20
time units in steps of 0.5 and prints the state every two time units.

```{r simulate}
regulation <- tf_theory("regulation-demo", "Arousal regulated by avoidance") |>
  tf_add_construct("arousal", "Physiological arousal", "bodily activation") |>
  tf_add_construct("threat", "Perceived threat", "appraised danger") |>
  tf_add_construct("avoidance", "Avoidance behaviour", "protective withdrawal") |>
  tf_add_proposition("p1", "arousal", "threat", "increases") |>
  tf_add_proposition("p2", "threat", "avoidance", "increases") |>
  tf_add_proposition("p3", "avoidance", "arousal", "decreases")

sim <- tf_simulate(regulation, steps = 40, dt = 0.5)
every_two <- seq(1, 41, by = 4)
trajectory <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sim$trajectory[every_two], unlist))
colnames(trajectory) <- unlist(sim$states)
data.frame(time = (every_two - 1) * sim$dt, trajectory)
```

Arousal falls first, pushed down by avoidance. Threat and avoidance rise briefly
and then follow it down, each later than the one before, and arousal later
climbs back above its starting value. The three constructs keep cycling, and at
the default gain of 1 and damping of 0.5 the swings neither grow nor fade.

Whether a feedback loop grows or settles is set by the gain against the
damping, neither of which the theory states. The loop of arousal and perceived
threat in the panic-network theory, closed by a `causes` proposition coupled
positively by assumption, grows at the defaults, a gain of 1 and a damping of
0.5, holds its level at a damping of 1 and settles above it. Time is in units
of `1/k`, and the window that `steps` and `dt` choose decides what is seen. The
last construct of a chain of five, which decays in the long run, shows only a
rise in the default window of one time unit.

```{r simulate-regime}
ends <- lapply(c(0.5, 1, 1.5), function(damping) {
  sim <- tf_simulate(v1, steps = 30, damping = damping)
  stats::setNames(sim$trajectory[[31]], unlist(sim$states))
})
data.frame(damping = c(0.5, 1, 1.5), do.call(rbind, ends))

chain <- tf_theory("chain", "A chain of five constructs")
for (i in 0:4) chain <- tf_add_construct(chain, paste0("c", i), paste0("C", i), "A state.")
for (i in 0:3) {
  chain <- tf_add_proposition(chain, paste0("p", i), paste0("c", i), paste0("c", i + 1),
                              "increases")
}
window <- function(steps) {
  last <- vapply(tf_simulate(chain, steps = steps)$trajectory, `[[`, numeric(1), 5L)
  c(time = steps * 0.1, end = last[[length(last)]], peak = max(last))
}
rbind(window(10), window(400))
```

A linear system has one equilibrium, or a continuum of them, and never two
separate ones, so it cannot show the alternative stable states that some
theories posit. `method = "euler"` takes fixed explicit steps, which stay close
to the solution only while `dt` is small against the network's rates. On the
regulation loop above, they inflate the oscillation, and `tf_simulate()` warns
when an Euler trajectory departs from the exact one by more than 5 per cent of
the larger of the exact value and the largest absolute starting value. `init`
sets the starting values, one number for every construct or a named list such
as `list(arousal = 1)`, which starts the constructs it leaves out at 0 and so
traces the response to an impulse. No data enter the trajectory, and it does
not show what the propositions imply beyond the signs it was built from.
